SLOPSQUATTING CHECK · RUNS ENTIRELY IN YOUR BROWSER, NO NETWORK CALL

Did an AI assistant just suggest a package that doesn't exist?

LLM code generators regularly suggest npm install commands for packages that were never published. A May 2025 USENIX Security study found 19.7% of packages recommended by 16 code-generating models did not exist at all. Attackers know this: they pre-register the exact names models are likely to hallucinate, so the next developer who copies the suggestion installs the attacker's package instead of getting an install error — a technique now called slopsquatting.

Paste your package.json below. Nothing is uploaded -- this page has no network call of any kind, on purpose. It flags names that look like a typo of a famous package; it cannot check whether a name actually exists on the registry right now. Get the free CLI below for that.

1. Paste your package.json

2. What looks like a near-miss of a famous package

DependencyFieldClose toEdit distance

Not checked (not a registry-backed specifier)

DependencySpecifier

Want the real answer, not a guess from a name list?

This page compares names against roughly 130 well-known packages hard-coded into it -- it has no way to know whether a name that isn't on that list actually exists. The CLI answers the question that actually matters: is this name registered at all, and if it is, does it look freshly squatted? Same zero-dependency shape as this portfolio's other supply-chain checkers.

node cli.mjs                     # scan ./package.json against the live registry
node cli.mjs path/to/package.json
node cli.mjs --json
node cli.mjs --strict            # also fail CI on a suspiciously new (but real) name

Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs -- Node 18+, nothing to install. It sends only each dependency's name to registry.npmjs.org, one read-only request per name -- the only network call anywhere in this tool.

Real, dated incidents that used exactly this mechanism

More: what is slopsquatting, and why doesn't a lockfile already protect you. See also how this compares to Socket, an ongoing registry-aware scanning service, and how this compares to just reading package.json by hand.

Common questions

What is slopsquatting?

Registering a package name that a large language model hallucinates in generated code. A May 2025 USENIX Security study found 19.7% of packages recommended by 16 code-generating models did not exist at all. If a developer copies an AI's install suggestion without checking, and an attacker has already registered that exact hallucinated name, the install silently succeeds against the attacker's package instead of failing.

Does this page check the live npm registry?

No, and deliberately so. This page never sends anything anywhere -- it only compares the names you paste against a short built-in list of about 130 extremely well-known packages, entirely in your browser. For the real question -- does this exact name exist right now, and if so how new and untrusted does it look -- use the companion CLI, which is the only part of this tool that touches the network, making one read-only request per dependency to registry.npmjs.org.

Is a flagged name proof of anything?

No. A near-miss of a famous package name can be a coincidence, an unrelated real package, or a genuine typosquat -- this tool cannot tell those apart, on the browser page or in the CLI. A flag means "read this one before you trust it", the same framing this portfolio's other supply-chain checkers use, never a verdict.

Is my dependency data uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the package.json you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere -- there is no fetch call in this page at all. The CLI reads your local file and sends only each dependency's name (never the whole file, never your code) to the public npm registry, one request per name.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It flags npm dependency names that resemble a hallucinated or typosquatted variant of a well-known package, or that fail a live registry existence/freshness check in the CLI -- it is not a malware scanner, not a security audit, and not a guarantee that an unflagged name is safe or a flagged one is malicious. It does not replace verifying a package yourself or a qualified security review. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

This page runs entirely in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over your dependency tree: Dependency Confusion Check flags --extra-index-url and unscoped-private-registry configuration mistakes behind the 2021 dependency-confusion attacks. And npm Lifecycle Script Check diffs two lockfile snapshots to name exactly which package just started running code at install time -- the mechanism behind Shai-Hulud.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-package-names-by-eye.html.text:
← Slopsquatting Check

Slopsquatting Check vs. Eyeballing package.json by Hand

Reading your own package.json works, and for a file you typed yourself, one dependency at a time, it can be the fastest check there is. It gets harder the moment the install command came from an AI assistant and you copied it rather than typed it -- you are now scanning a list of names for a one- or two-character difference from something you already trust, which is exactly the kind of change a fast read skips over. This free tool checks every name at once against a known-package list, entirely offline in your browser.

What each approach is for

Reading it by eye means opening package.json, or the diff that added a line to it, and recognizing whether each dependency name looks right. For a short file, or a name you typed yourself and already know, this can be the whole job -- no tool needed.

This checker parses the dependencies and devDependencies you paste and compares every name's edit distance against roughly 130 extremely well-known packages, entirely in your browser, with no network call of any kind. It flags a name that looks like a one- or two-character typo of something famous -- the exact shape a slopsquatted or typosquatted name takes -- in a fraction of a second, whether the file has three dependencies or thirty.

Where each approach earns its keep.
SituationBetter fit
A handful of dependencies you typed yourself and already know by name.Reading by eye -- often faster than pasting the file in here.
An AI assistant's install suggestion you copied without typing it yourself.This checker -- it compares the exact spelling instantly instead of relying on a read that trusts the name because it "looks right."
A longer package.json, or a name that is not close to anything on this tool's known-package list.Both have limits here: a manual reader can miss a subtle near-miss among many lines, and this offline page has no way to know whether an unlisted name exists at all.
Whether a name that isn't a near-miss actually exists on the registry, and how old it is.The companion CLI -- it makes the one live, read-only check this offline page deliberately does not.

Treat this checker as a fast first pass across every name in the file, and a manual read as the judgment call on what a flagged (or not-flagged-but-unfamiliar) name is actually for. This page names no company or product being compared against -- reading a file by eye is a habit, not a competitor.

Run the free offline check

Common questions

Isn't reading my own package.json always going to be more reliable?

For a file you wrote by hand, one dependency at a time, it can be. It gets harder the moment an AI assistant wrote the install command for you and you copied it without typing the name yourself -- you are now reading a name you did not choose, looking for a one- or two-character difference from a package you already trust, which is precisely the kind of change a fast read skips over. This tool compares every name in the file against roughly 130 well-known packages in a fraction of a second, the same check every time, no matter how tired the read is.

What can a manual read catch that this tool cannot?

Context this tool has no access to: whether a name looks right for what the project actually needs, whether a teammate mentioned adding it, or whether it showed up in a diff nobody expected. The offline check only compares spelling against a short known-package list -- it has no opinion on whether a name that isn't a near-miss of something famous is safe, and it cannot tell you whether the name was ever intentional.

Does this replace checking the package for real?

No. A flag from this page is a prompt to read that one dependency before trusting it -- the same read you would otherwise be doing for every dependency, just narrowed to the names worth a second look. And the offline page cannot tell you whether an unflagged name actually exists on the registry at all; that is what the companion CLI checks, with one read-only request per name against registry.npmjs.org.

Why would a hallucinated name pass a careful manual read?

Because it is designed to. A model hallucinates names that sound exactly like something that should exist -- a plausible scoped package, a common utility-library shape -- and an attacker who has already registered that name is counting on a reviewer recognizing the shape and moving on. A near-miss of a package you already trust, buried among two dozen genuine dependencies, is the case a quick visual pass is built to miss and an edit-distance comparison is built to catch.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It flags npm dependency names that resemble a hallucinated or typosquatted variant of a well-known package -- it is not a malware scanner, not a security audit, and not a guarantee that an unflagged name is safe. It does not replace verifying a package yourself or a qualified security review. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime or that a URL will keep working.

This page runs entirely in your browser. The package.json you paste is never uploaded, and this page makes no live comparison against any manual read -- it is a static page describing the tradeoff, not a live scan of any file. We count only anonymous local feature events, never people or file content, with an opt-out on the checker page. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — optional support: GitHub Sponsors. Refusing does not change the checker.

vs-socket.html.text:
← Slopsquatting Check

This checker vs. Socket

Two different layers: Socket watches your dependency graph and the public registries on an ongoing basis for 70+ risk types, typosquatting among them. This tool makes one on-demand, read-only registry request per dependency to answer one narrow question — does this exact name exist, and does it look freshly squatted — no account, no ongoing service.

What each product is for

Socket is a supply-chain security platform. Its own site describes deep package inspection that characterizes what a dependency actually does, rather than relying only on known-vulnerability databases, connected through a GitHub app, a CLI, and a browser extension. It flags more than 70 categories of risk across npm, PyPI, and other ecosystems — typosquatting, malware, hidden or obfuscated code, and permission creep among them — and monitors changes to a project's dependency manifest on an ongoing basis. It is free for public, open-source use, and Socket's own site lists paid Team, Business, and Enterprise tiers for private-repository and organization use; today's specific prices and contract terms are not repeated here, since this session cannot verify them live against Socket's own site — only its well-documented product shape is described.

This tool does one narrower thing, on demand rather than continuously: given a package.json, it makes one read-only GET request per dependency to registry.npmjs.org and reports whether the name resolves at all, and if it does, whether it was published very recently with almost no version history — the specific fingerprint of a name freshly registered after being hallucinated by an AI assistant or guessed by a typosquatter. It has no account, no ongoing service, and no GitHub app, and it does not attempt any of Socket's other 69-plus risk categories.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want continuous, registry-aware scanning of my whole dependency graph for malware, typosquats, permission creep, and dozens of other supply-chain risks.Socket — that is the ongoing, cross-ecosystem job it is built for.
I want to know right now, for free, whether a specific dependency name actually exists and whether it looks freshly squatted.This tool — one command, one read-only request per dependency, no account.
I want a GitHub app or browser extension that watches every future pull request for newly introduced risky dependencies.Socket — this tool has no memory between runs and no ongoing monitoring.
I want a fully offline check with zero network calls of any kind, even at the cost of not knowing whether a name actually exists.This tool's browser page — it flags near-misses of well-known names locally and never touches the network; the live check is CLI-only.
I want to know whether a specific package has ever shown malicious behavior at runtime.Socket — this tool only checks a name's existence and registration recency, never behavior.

A team can reasonably run both: Socket for continuous, registry-aware defense across many risk types, and this tool as a fast, zero-account gate specifically for the AI-hallucination pattern — in CI, at release time, or by hand. This page does not evaluate Socket's detection accuracy and makes no claim about it either way — it only describes Socket's documented product shape and states what this tool does differently. Socket catching a live malicious package and this tool flagging a freshly squatted name are two different signals; neither replaces the other, and a clean result from either one is not a supply-chain security guarantee.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in. The browser page is a static page with no network call of any kind; the CLI is a single stdlib-only script that makes one read-only registry request per dependency.

Common questions

Does Socket already catch a hallucinated or freshly squatted package name?

Socket's own site describes deep package inspection and real-time monitoring across more than 70 risk categories, typosquatting among them, by watching your dependency graph against live registry data through a GitHub app, CLI, or browser extension. That is ongoing, registry-aware monitoring across many risk types at once. This tool does one narrower, on-demand thing: for each dependency in a package.json you hand it, it makes one read-only request to the public npm registry and reports whether the name exists at all, and if it does, whether it was published suspiciously recently with almost no version history.

Should I use this tool or Socket?

They work at different layers, and a team can reasonably run both. Socket runs on an ongoing basis against your dependency graph and the public registries, watching for a live attack across dozens of package-behavior signals, as a service that is free for public open-source use and offers paid plans for private and organization use, per Socket's own site; connecting it needs a GitHub app, CLI, or browser extension. This tool answers one narrower question, on demand, with nothing to connect: does this exact name exist, and does it look freshly squatted? Free, no account, one read-only request per dependency.

what-is-slopsquatting.html.text:
← Back to Slopsquatting Check

What is slopsquatting, and why doesn't a lockfile already protect you?

Code-generating LLMs suggest npm install or pip install commands as part of their answers. A May 2025 USENIX Security study, "We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs," tested 16 models and found that 19.7% of the packages they recommended did not exist at all — 21.7% for open-source models versus 5.2% for proprietary ones — and collected more than 205,000 unique hallucinated package names across the study. That is not a rare edge case; it is roughly one in five suggestions from the weaker end of that range.

An attacker who wants to distribute malware does not need to guess at random: they can generate code with the same class of models, collect the names those models hallucinate, and register the most repeated ones on the real registry ahead of time. The next developer who pastes the AI's suggested install command gets the attacker's package instead of an install error. Security researcher Andrew Nesbitt and later researchers named this slopsquatting — a play on typosquatting, where the "typo" is one the model made for you.

Two real cases

CaseDateWhat happened
huggingface-cli2023Security researcher Bar Lanyado registered a package under a name he had seen an LLM hallucinate and published it empty, as a proof of concept. It was downloaded more than 30,000 times in three months, and the same hallucinated name turned up inside an Alibaba research repository's own README.
PhantomRaven campaignflagged October 2025 (active since November 2022)Koi Security and DCODX documented 100+ malicious npm packages distributed under slopsquatted and typosquatted names; CrowdStrike assessed the malware itself was written with the help of an LLM. The packages stole authentication tokens, CI/CD secrets, and GitHub credentials.

Why a lockfile doesn't already catch this

A package-lock.json pins a name and version that already resolved successfully once. That tells you nothing about how the name got there in the first place — it is equally consistent with "this was always a real, well-known package" and with "an AI hallucinated this name, an attacker had already squatted it by the time someone ran npm install, and the lockfile faithfully recorded the attacker's package as if it were the intended one." The moment that actually matters is the first install of a newly added dependency, before it is ever committed — which is also the one moment a lockfile, by definition, cannot yet describe.

What actually helps

Two independent, narrow checks, neither of which needs to trust a model to grade its own homework:

  • Does the name exist at all? If it does not, that is either a genuine typo in your own manifest or a name nobody has claimed yet — worth fixing or verifying before it becomes true by someone else's registration.
  • If it exists, does it look freshly squatted? A name registered days ago with one version published is a different risk profile from a package with years of history and dozens of releases, even though both "exist."
node cli.mjs package.json          # both checks, one read-only request per dependency
node cli.mjs package.json --strict # also fail CI on a suspiciously new (but real) name

Get the free browser check and CLI — Node 18+, zero dependencies, MIT licensed. See also how this compares to Socket, an ongoing registry-aware scanning service, and how this compares to reading package.json by hand.

Common questions

Doesn't npm just fail if the package doesn't exist?

Only until someone registers the name. The risk window is between an AI assistant hallucinating a name and an attacker claiming it -- before that, install fails loudly and safely; after it, install succeeds quietly against the attacker's package, and nothing about the failure you would have expected ever happens.

If my lockfile already resolves the name, am I safe?

A lockfile records a name and version that already resolved once, which means either it was always a real package, or it was a hallucinated name that had already been squatted by the time someone ran install and committed the lockfile -- a lockfile cannot tell those two apart after the fact. The moment that matters is the first install of a newly added name, before it is ever committed.

Why not just always tell the AI assistant to double check?

Some tools do, and it helps, but it relies on the same model that hallucinated the name to also catch its own mistake, which the USENIX study's own numbers argue against relying on alone. A check against the registry itself does not depend on the model being right twice.

No warranty. Provided free and as-is; not a security audit, not a malware scanner, not a guarantee. See the tool's own disclaimer for the full text.
